soil-env-058.title: Soil degradation: when a stable soil starts to slide
soil-env-058.text: Over the last 30 years, the quality of 33% of the world's pastureland has deteriorated. So has that of 25% of its arable land and 23% of its forests, and 3.2 billion people depend on this land. Soil degradation is the name for that slide. Strictly, it is a regressive change in which a stable soil loses its equilibrium. More broadly, it is any disturbance to a soil judged harmful or undesirable. Degradation, also called pedolysis, departs from the natural course of soil formation. Secondary plant communities replace the mature vegetation, and the amount and makeup of humus change with them. Degradation is tied directly to human activity, while its companion process, {{ref:soil-env-059}}, is driven mainly by erosion. Erosion is still the main factor, acting through water erosion, wind erosion, and chemical and physical decline. Roads add impermeable surfaces that shed runoff and soil. Grazing too many animals, monoculture, row cropping, tillage, crop removal and land-use conversion all speed erosion. Age matters too. Soils naturally climb to high productivity and then decline as mineral nutrients are removed, so older soils are more vulnerable to damage people cause. On farms, erosion, compaction, lowered fertility and contamination remain serious concerns.

soil-env-062.title: Land degradation: when land loses its power to provide
soil-env-062.text: By one 2007 estimate, up to 40% of the world's agricultural land was seriously degraded. The UN has warned that the global economy could lose $23 trillion by 2050. Land degradation is the process behind those numbers: land growing less healthy and productive through human activities or natural conditions. Definitions differ in emphasis. The 2005 Millennium Ecosystem Assessment called it the reduction or loss of the biological or economic productivity of {{ref:soil-env-077}}. The FAO describes a persistent decline in the land's ability to sustain ecosystem functions and services, driven by deforestation, too many grazing animals and unsustainable farming. People are usually the main cause, above all through unsustainable land management. Natural hazards are excluded, though people can indirectly affect floods and wildfires. The impacts range from subtle productivity losses to the complete abandonment of farmland. Degraded land grows less food and loses species. It can also lose its natural capacity to store and filter water, leading to water scarcity, so both food security and water security suffer. Judgments differ, too. A steep, rainy slope worries scientists about erosion, but it may promise farmers high yields.

soil-env-065.title: What drives land degradation, near and far
soil-env-065.text: More than 1 660 Mha of land, over 10 percent of the world's land area, has been degraded by unsustainable land use and management. More than 60% of it is cropland and pasture. Researchers sort the causes into two tiers. Proximate drivers are biophysical factors and unsustainable land management. Underlying drivers are social, economic and institutional. Agriculture, deforestation and climate change top the list, with clearcutting and overlogging among the ways land is cleared. On farms, leaving soil bare after harvest and deep plowing deplete nutrients. Areas under conventional tillage degrade 5-10 times faster than no-till areas. Monocultures, grazing beyond the livestock carrying capacity and inappropriate irrigation add to the damage. So does pollution from littering, urbanization, mining, oil spills, pesticides, herbicides, fertilizers and animal waste. Crowding alone is not the culprit. High population density is not always linked to degradation; it is people's practices that degrade a landscape.

soil-env-063.title: How much of Earth's land is wearing out
soil-env-063.text: Every year about 120,000 km2 of productive land is degraded, an area roughly the size of Greece. The cause is exploitation without planning for long-term sustainability. Erosion from farm fields runs 11 to 20 times faster than soil forms under no-tillage, and more than 100 times faster under conventional tillage. Global tallies vary with who counts and when. The IPCC's 2019 Special Report on Climate Change and Land put about a quarter of Earth's ice-free land under human-induced degradation, with medium confidence. In 2014 the UN estimated that around 30% of land was degraded, with around 3.2 billion people living on it. In 2024 it claimed that 75% of soils are degraded to some extent, a share that might reach 90% by 2050 if trends continue. In 2025 around 1.7 billion people lived where degradation causes sizeable crop yield losses, nearly 1 billion of them in middle-income countries. Eastern and Southern Asia hold the largest affected populations, pairing a large accumulated degradation debt with high population densities. In 2021, two-thirds of Africa's productive land was claimed to be severely affected.

soil-env-067.title: The bill for degraded land: harvests, water and lives
soil-env-067.text: Each year the world loses 76 billion tons of soil, at a cost of about US$400 billion. Land degradation as a whole is estimated to cost US$44 billion a year. The first loss is productive capacity, temporary or permanent, seen as lost biomass, changed vegetation cover or depleted soil nutrients. Slight degradation cuts yield potential by 10% and moderate degradation by 10–50%. Severely degraded soils have lost more than 50% of their potential. Most of them are in developing countries; in Africa yields fall 2–40%, an average loss of 8.2% for the continent. Eroded soil also carries nitrogen, phosphorus, farm chemicals and heavy metals into surface water, clouding it and risking {{ref:soil-env-020}}. Degradation disturbs soil microbes, removes mature vegetation and shrinks animal habitat, so biodiversity falls. Floods degrade soil, and degraded soil causes floods. Scarce farmland breeds conflict: all except 3 internal conflicts in African states in the 1990s are linked to competition for it.

soil-env-070.title: Sustainable land management: keeping land in working order
soil-env-070.text: Reverse just 10% of human-induced cropland degradation, and an additional 154 million people a year could be fed. Restoring abandoned cropland could feed between 292 and 476 million. Sustainable land management chases such gains by managing land to prevent and reverse degradation while conserving soil and water. Its actions fall broadly into three groups: prevention, mitigation and restoration. It raises soil moisture and infiltration while cutting runoff, erosion and flood discharge, which supports water security. Regenerative agriculture pursues the same goal through continuous ground cover, minimal soil disturbance, diverse crop rotations and rotational grazing. Degradation also harms pastures and wider ecosystem services, which are public goods, so restoring land requires collective action. Public awareness, education and outreach help communities adopt such practices and act as stewards of the land.

soil-env-093.title: Soil sealing: burying living ground under asphalt
soil-env-093.text: Pave a field and its soil stops working almost for good. Soil sealing is the loss of soil resources when land is covered over for housing, roads or other construction. Topsoil is covered or replaced by asphalt and cement, and the layers below are compacted. The loss of the soil's ecosystem services is mostly irreversible. Sealing is a serious form of land take, and together they destroy the soil's biological, physical and chemical functions completely. Water suffers first. Sealed ground becomes the kind of surface described in {{ref:soil-water-231}}: it hinders infiltration and increases surface runoff. Sealing for underground construction also alters water movement and weakens the soil's ability to purify water. Heat-absorbing concrete and asphalt, with no vegetation to cool them, create urban heat islands. Fertile farmland under buildings no longer produces food, and countries with fast-growing populations and economies are losing notable areas this way. Sealing fragments habitats and causes soil biodiversity loss, made worse by falling soil carbon, nitrogen and respiration. It also removes urban green spaces that offer recreation, learning and a sense of belonging. Researchers assess sealing with raindrop impact tests in the field and laboratory, and with indices such as the NDVI and the Normalized Difference Built-up Index.

soil-env-101.title: Land consumption: open country that never comes back
soil-env-101.text: From 1990 to 2000 the United States consumed 1.4 million hectares of open space. Germany consumes more than 70 hectares every day. Land consumption is the conversion of land with healthy soil and intact habitats into industrial farmland, roads and, above all, urban settlements. The European Environment Agency names three such activities. One is expanding built-up area. Another is extending the land exploited for farming, forestry and other uses. The third is over-intensive exploitation of farm and forest land. Because these changes are virtually irreversible, the term land loss is also used. Erosion and the spread of desert land, covered in {{ref:soil-env-072}}, also cause land loss, mostly traceable to people. Land take in 21 EU countries reached about 1.2 million hectares over 1990–2006. The damage includes lost habitat, lost or contaminated topsoil, compaction that eradicates soil life, and impervious surfaces that disrupt water and biogeochemical cycles. Consumption also reaches abroad. A region's land footprint is the area at home and abroad needed for what it consumes. It can far exceed the region's own land, and Europe depends most on such imported land. Yet the land economy still lacks full-cost accounting for the long-term costs of environmental degradation.

soil-env-060.title: From bare rock to climax: a soil grows up
soil-env-060.text: On bare rock, lichens and mosses arrive first, then herbs, shrubs and finally forest. Beneath them a humus-bearing A horizon forms, then mineral B horizons. This evolution is succession, and its endpoint is a steady balance between soil and vegetation, the highest development the environment can produce. Some ecologists call it the climax, others the natural potential. The journey takes tens to thousands of years for fast soils with only an A horizon, and more than a million years for slow ones. Regional climate and biome set the general course, while parent rock and local drainage explain specialized cases such as peat bogs.

soil-env-059.title: Soil retrogression: sliding back toward bare rock
soil-env-059.text: A soil at its climax tends to stay stable. Its vegetation supplies humus, moves material upward and shields the ground from water and wind, while roots bind the particles together. Destroy that cover on a large scale, by an avalanche or by people, and erosion strips away the upper horizons. This reversion toward pioneer conditions is soil retrogression. It can be partial, or total, leaving bare rock. Clearing a sloping site exposed to violent rains can destroy its soil completely. People often drive it more slowly. Clearing, excessive cutting, forest grazing and litter raking replace the climax vegetation, as when broadleaf forest gives way to moorland or pine plantations. Many such cases stem from very old practices. Recovery is possible. After a disturbance, secondary succession usually takes over, and it runs much faster than primary succession because a soil already exists. Succession and regression can follow each other over short intervals under human action, or over long ones as the climate changes.

soil-env-061.title: Rebuilding a degraded soil with a dose of clay
soil-env-061.text: No technique can fully restore a soil, with its fauna and flora, that took more than a thousand years to build. Rebuilding still helps, chiefly by improving structure, adding organic matter and limiting runoff. On low-clay soils in northern Thailand, one application of 200 kg of bentonite clay per rai (6.26 rai = 1 hectare) helped hold water and nutrients. Yields rose by an average of 73%. A 2008 survey of 250 farmers in the northeast found output 18% higher among clay users, and some switched to vegetables, which need more fertile soil. On degraded sandy soils, bentonite also cut the risk of crop failure in drought years.

soil-env-077.title: Drylands: where evaporation spends nearly every drop
soil-env-077.text: Drylands cover 41.3% of Earth's land surface and are home to more than 2 billion people. They are zones defined by scarce water, where precipitation is balanced by evaporation and plant evapotranspiration. UNEP counts tropical and temperate areas whose score on a dryness measure, explained in {{ref:soil-env-206}}, falls below 0.65. They come in four sub-types: dry sub-humid, semi-arid, arid and hyper-arid. The UN convention described in {{ref:soil-env-100}} leaves hyper-arid zones out. Drylands cover 66% of Africa, 40% of Asia, 24% of Europe and 15% of Latin America, and include 45% of the world's agricultural land. Of all drylands, 72% lie in developing countries, as does almost all hyper-arid land. Arid lands make up about 10% of the world's land. Hyper-arid lands cover about 8% and get irregular rain barely above 100 mm. Unlike more humid biomes, drylands move water mostly as above-ground runoff. They are among the ecosystems most vulnerable to climate and land-use change. From 1982 to 2015, 12.6% of them degraded because of human-caused climate change. Pressure to farm marginal drylands also brings too many grazing animals, land exhaustion and overdrafting of groundwater to many poorer countries.

soil-env-072.title: Desertification: fertile land turned to desert
soil-env-072.text: Some 6 to 12 million square kilometres of land are affected by desertification, and a billion people are threatened by its further spread. Desertification is the gradual degradation of fertile land into arid desert through natural processes and human activities combined. Its immediate cause is the loss of most vegetation. Drought, climatic shifts, acid rain, tillage, grazing by too many animals and cutting forests for fuel or building materials can strip it, alone or together. Plant cover matters enormously: in many environments erosion and runoff fall exponentially as cover increases. Once the cover goes, unprotected dry topsoil blows away or washes off in flash floods. The infertile layers left behind bake in the sun into an unproductive hardpan. Wind erosion, especially when people raise it far above natural rates, is a major source, and erosion can end in desertification. Some 10–20% of drylands are estimated to be degraded. The worst-hit areas are the Sahel in Africa, the Gobi Desert and Mongolia in Asia, and parts of South America. The effects include sand and dust storms, food insecurity and poverty, and desertification is recognized as a major threat to biodiversity. Remedies include improving soil quality, greening deserts, managing grazing, reforestation and afforestation.

soil-env-100.title: The UN treaty built to fight desertification
soil-env-100.text: Only one internationally legally binding framework addresses desertification: the United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification, or UNCCD. It is also the only convention to stem directly from Agenda 21 of the Rio Conference. Adopted in Paris on 17 June 1994, it entered into force in December 1996. It works through national action programmes backed by international cooperation, built on participation, partnership and decentralization. These National Action Programmes, drawn up with local communities, set out practical steps for specific ecosystems. The convention has 197 parties: all 193 UN member states plus the European Union. Canada withdrew in 2013 and rejoined in 2017. The Conference of the Parties is its supreme decision-making body, meeting annually from 1997 to 2001 and every two years since. A Committee on Science and Technology reviews data on the natural and human causes. The 2018–2030 Strategic Framework, adopted in 2017, aims to restore ecosystems, support {{ref:soil-env-071}}, improve living conditions and strengthen drought resilience. At COP16 in Riyadh in December 2024, more than US$12 billion was pledged. How much the 2006 International Year of Deserts and Desertification, declared to publicise the convention, achieved is still debated.

soil-env-076.title: A warming world grows its drylands
soil-env-076.text: By the end of this century, drylands could cover 50% or 56% of the continents, up from 38% in the late 20th century. Those figures come from RCP 4.5 and RCP 8.5, two scenarios of future greenhouse gas concentrations. Most of the growth is expected in southwest North America, the northern fringe of Africa, southern Africa and Australia. The change is already under way. A 2020 attribution study found that 6% of the world's drylands underwent desertification between 1982 and 2015. Unsustainable land use drove it, compounded by human-caused climate change. Despite average global greening, that climate change has degraded 12.6% of drylands, or 5.43 million km2. It affects 213 million people, 93% of them in developing economies. Research is complex, because no single metric captures every aspect of desertification.

soil-env-084.title: Why halting desertification is harder than it looks
soil-env-084.text: The know-how to fight desertification exists; the incentives often do not. Sustainable practices can cost individual farmers more than they gain, even when society and the environment benefit. Lack of political will and of funding for land reclamation also holds programmes back. Still, countermeasures keep coming. Some countries have biodiversity action plans to protect endangered plants and animals from desertification. The FAO launched its Drylands Restoration Initiative in 2012, and in 2015 it published global guidelines for restoring degraded dryland forests and landscapes. UN Sustainable Development Goal 15 adds global advocacy for combating desertification and restoring affected land.

soil-env-086.title: Greening the desert, one kind of desert at a time
soil-env-086.text: In Niger, farmers have reclaimed some 30,000 square kilometers of degraded land with the method described in {{ref:soil-env-087}}. Desert greening is the reclamation of deserts and desertified land, with methods matched to each kind of desert. Ethiopia's Humbo Assisted Regeneration Project uses the same techniques. It is paid for by the World Bank's BioCarbon Fund, which backs carbon sequestration in forests and farmland. Salt flats in Saudi Arabia's Rub' al Khali are among the most promising sites for seawater agriculture, which needs no freshwater and little energy. The best-known approach is large tree-planting belts. China's version appears in {{ref:soil-env-088}}, and the African Union's belt along the Sahara in {{ref:soil-env-089}}.

soil-env-085.title: Fixing, watering and feeding desert soils
soil-env-085.text: Contour trenches 150 m long and 1 m deep, edged with stone walls, follow a slope's contour so water cannot flow downhill and cause erosion. Such techniques supply water to dryland soils, fix them in place and enrich them. Shelter belts, woodlots and windbreaks of trees and bushes hold the soil, reducing erosion and evapotranspiration, while sand fences control drifting sand. Short of water, clay soils can consolidate instead of staying porous; techniques such as zaï or tillage still let crops be planted. Plants restore fertility, chiefly nitrogen-fixing legumes, succulents such as Opuntia, and crops and trees such as grains, barley, beans and dates. Nitrogen-rich fertilizer works too, but its cost deters smallholders, so India, Zambia and Malawi subsidize it. Research centres are inoculating arid-zone trees with mycorrhizal fungi, which greatly enlarge the root surface that gathers nutrients. Models suggest bioengineered soil microbes, especially photosynthesizers, could strengthen the cooperative loops between microbes and dryland plants.

soil-env-066.title: Climate change and degraded land feed each other
soil-env-066.text: From 1961 to 2013, the area of drylands in drought grew by more than 1% a year. Climate change worsens land degradation, especially on low-lying coasts, river deltas, drylands and permafrost. Heavy rainfall and extreme weather make erosion, soil degradation and compaction more likely. Rising seas can flood deltas and low islands with seawater, raising salinity until farming becomes impossible. The 2022 IPCC report found degradation responding more directly to climate change, with all types of erosion and soil organic matter decline increasing. The loop runs both ways: degraded land releases greenhouse gases, which worsen climate change. People bear the cost. In 2015 about 500,000,000 people lived in areas that had undergone desertification during the 1980s–2000s. Some 74% of the world's poor are reported to be directly affected by land degradation.

soil-env-091.title: Solar panels that help desert soil recover
soil-env-091.text: The Kubuqi Desert gets around 300 mm of rain a year, yet a 2025 study found its soil recovering under solar farms. Microbial counts, soil quality and nutrients improved most under integrated agrivoltaic systems, which pair solar panels with planted vegetation. Panel shade cut soil temperature and evaporation. The panels also acted as windbreaks that kept sand from burying plants, and with the vegetation they created a better microclimate. A 2 GW project in Inner Mongolia plans to apply this at scale to restore vegetation, stabilize dunes and weaken dust storms.

soil-env-073.title: More than 100 ways to define desertification
soil-env-073.text: By 2005, desertification had more than 100 formal definitions, and the proper one is still considerably disputed. The UNCCD defines it as land degradation in arid, semi-arid and dry sub-humid regions, resulting from factors including climatic variations and human activities. That wording ties desertification to land use and management and highlights its economic, social and environmental implications. The original idea, that it meant the physical expansion of deserts, has been rejected as the concept evolved. Sub-groupings such as 'man-made desert' and 'non-pattern desert' remain disputed too.

soil-env-078.title: Desertification raises the dust
soil-env-078.text: Global annual dust emissions rose 25% between the late nineteenth century and the present day. As desertification leaves more loose material for the wind, storms of sand and dust grow more frequent. In the Middle East, long-term rainfall decline has lowered soil moisture and plant cover, and dust storms are becoming more frequent and intense. They contribute to pneumonia and asthma, pollute open water and can halt most transport. Airborne dust also scatters sunlight and warms the atmosphere, shortening cloud lifetimes and reducing rainfall, which can worsen desertification in turn.

soil-env-079.title: Drylands feed the world, and they are shrinking
soil-env-079.text: Drylands hold 44% of agricultural land, and that land supplies 60% of the world's food production. Desertification threatens this supply by shrinking the land that can be farmed sustainably. Food demand keeps growing with population while the farmland shrinks, so demand may soon exceed supply. The squeeze has already turned violent. Climate change, land degradation and population growth have worsened herder–farmer conflicts in Nigeria, Sudan, Mali and other Sahel countries.

soil-env-080.title: Desertification and the road from farm to slum
soil-env-080.text: In sub-Saharan Africa, environmental refugees are projected to rise from 14 million in 2010 to nearly 200 million by 2050. Desertification deepens poverty by lowering what dryland farms and pastures produce. Investors avoid low-potential arid zones, and without infrastructure, markets and suitable techniques most such zones are left out of development. When rural land can no longer support its people, they migrate to cities, particularly in Africa, creating unemployment and slums. In Mongolia, where 90% of the land is fragile dryland, many herders move to the city for work.

soil-env-082.title: The Gobi, Earth's fastest-growing desert
soil-env-082.text: Each year the Gobi turns over 3,600 km2 of grassland into wasteland, and large sand dunes are forming only 70 km from Beijing. It is spreading across northern China and southern Mongolia faster than any other desert on Earth. About 13% of Mongolia's desertification is put down to natural factors. The rest comes mainly from too many grazing animals and erosion of cultivated soils, and over 70% of the country's land is degraded. From 1940 to 2015 Mongolia's mean air temperature rose by 2.24 °C while precipitation fell by 7%. Cashmere exports added pressure: herds shifted from sheep to goats, which eat roots and flowers and so degrade grazing land.

openers.degradation-and-desertification: Soil can go backward. Left alone, a soil and its plants evolve together toward a steady balance, the highest development their environment can produce. Destroy the vegetation, and erosion can strip the upper horizons and push the soil back toward its pioneer beginnings. This chapter follows that decline from soil degradation to land degradation, with its many human and natural drivers and its costs in lost harvests, polluted water, vanishing species and money. It covers soil sealed under housing and roads, the drylands described in {{ref:soil-env-077}}, and the practices that prevent damage, reverse it and rebuild degraded soil.
